snippets.text: MR is a heterogeneous disease entity with diverse etiologies involving the mitral-valve leaflets, annulus, chordae tendineae, papillary muscles, and LV geometry. The major causes of MR include myxomatous degeneration manifesting as MVP or ruptured chordae, rheumatic heart disease, IE, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, MAC, dilated cardiomyopathy, and ischemic heart disease. Given its multifactorial nature, accurate identification of the underlying mechanisms is essential for optimal management.

snippets.text: Stable angina, also known as typical angina or angina pectoris, is a symptom of myocardial ischemia. Stable angina is characterized by chest discomfort or anginal equivalent that is provoked with exertion and alleviated at rest or with nitroglycerin. This is often 1 of the first manifestations or warning signs of underlying coronary disease. Angina affects 10 million people in the United States (US); given this, it is important to recognize the signs and symptoms and appropriately risk stratify and manage these individuals.[1]

snippets.text: Temporally, stable angina is differentiated from unstable angina by its chronicity and reproducibility with exertion. Symptoms will typically last for minutes (not seconds or hours) and after a predictable amount of exertion before being relieved with rest. If the stable, chronic nature of angina changes, where it occurs with less exertion, last for a longer duration of time, or becomes more severe, then urgent evaluation for unstable angina needs to be performed.

snippets.text: Five of the 24 included studies compared CCTA with different imaging techniques in patients with stable angina [Figure 3]. In patients with stable coronary disease, the CT coronary angiography in patients with suspected angina due to coronary heart disease (SCOT-HEART) study observed that revascularization rates tended to be higher in the CCTA group compared to SC, although this finding was not statistically significant (P = 0.0611). Min et al., however, reported a statistically significant higher revascularization rate following CCTA compared to MPI (P = 0.03). In two studies, CCTA had either similar rates of subsequent invasive procedures compared to MPI (P = 0.19) or even lower rates (P = 0.041). snippets.text: Angina pectoris refers to the experience of retrosternal chest pain, pressure, or discomfort that may be exacerbated by exertion or emotional stress. While angina may be relieved by rest and nitroglycerin, which would be categorized as stable angina, angina not relieved by these factors is categorized as unstable angina. Unstable angina may be a predictor for cardiac events and can lead to serious morbidity if not properly identified and treated. Angina is caused by an imbalance between oxygen supply and demand in the heart. Most commonly, this can be associated with coronary artery disease where there is an atherosclerotic plaque narrowing the lumen of the blood vessel supplying oxygen and nutrients to the heart. With nearly 10 million adults in the USA experiencing stable angina, the first-line diagnostic test with a high sensitivity and comparable specificity is coronary CT angiography. Thus, ensuring a thorough diagnostic workup for any type of chest pain is crucial to avoid misdiagnoses of severe cardiac events, such as an acute myocardial infarction or an aortic dissection.
